title: Route Handlers and Proxy
summary: Answer HTTP requests with Route Handlers, run code before every route with proxy.ts, and set cookies and headers where each belongs.
intro: Pages answer with HTML, and Server Actions answer your own forms. Some requests need neither: a payment service telling your shop an order was paid, a phone app asking for products as JSON, a feed reader asking for your news as RSS. And some decisions come before any page runs, like sending visitors with no session to the login page. This lesson covers both ends. Route Handlers answer HTTP requests with any response you build, and `proxy.ts` sees each request before routing. Then it shows where cookies, CORS, and caching headers belong, how to run work after the response has gone, and how to catch every server error in one place.

steps.title: Route Handlers answer HTTP requests
steps.body:
Every endpoint so far has belonged to a page: its HTML, its RSC payload, or its form's action. A **Route Handler** is an endpoint with no page at all. You get the request, and you build the response, with whatever status, headers, and body it needs. It's the closest Next.js comes to a small API server, and it uses the same `Request` and `Response` objects that `fetch` uses in the browser.

## route.ts

A folder in `app/` becomes a URL, as the routing lesson showed, and a `page.tsx` in it makes that URL a page. A `route.ts` makes it an endpoint instead. Inside it, you export a function named after each HTTP method you want to answer: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, or `OPTIONS`. The first example, `app/api/products/[slug]/route.ts`, answers `GET /api/products/trail-pack-45`.

A folder holds a `page.tsx` or a `route.ts`, never both, since each takes every request to its URL. Teams put their handlers under `app/api/` so they never collide with pages. `api` is only a folder name, with no special meaning.

A method you don't export gets `405 Method Not Allowed`. `OPTIONS` comes for free: Next.js answers it with an `Allow` header that lists your methods. `HEAD`, which asks for the headers alone, comes free with `GET`. The third example shows both.

## Requests and responses

The handler receives a **Request** and returns a **Response**, the same objects you used with `fetch` in the web course, now on the server's side of the conversation. `Response.json(data, { status })` turns data into JSON and sets the `Content-Type` header for you. `new Response(body, { status, headers })` builds anything else: text, XML, a file, or a stream.

Next.js actually passes a `NextRequest`, a Request with two extras:

- `request.nextUrl`, the URL already parsed, so `request.nextUrl.searchParams.get("category")` reads the `cooking` in `?category=cooking`.
- `request.cookies`, to read a cookie by name.

## Params and the body

The handler's second argument holds the route's dynamic segments. As with a page, `params` is a promise you await. `RouteContext<"/api/products/[slug]">` types it from the route's path, a type Next.js generates for you the same way it generates `PageProps`.

A request body can be read once, with the method that fits it:

- `await request.json()` for JSON.
- `await request.formData()` for a posted form.
- `await request.text()` for the raw text, which you need when you check a signature, as the next part does.

Everything in the body came from the caller, so check it with zod before you use it, as the Server Actions lesson did.

## Prerendered, or run on every request

With Cache Components on, a `GET` handler follows the same rule as a page. If it reads nothing about the request, Next.js runs it once during `next build` and saves the answer, so every caller gets that same prerendered response. This course's app found that out the hard way: a test handler that threw an error, and read nothing from its request, made the build itself fail with Error occurred prerendering page "/api/boom".

A handler runs on every request when it has a dynamic segment with no prerendered values, or reads the request: `request.nextUrl`, its headers, `cookies()`, or `await connection()`, which says outright that this code needs a live request. The build's route table marks those handlers ƒ. Other methods, like `POST`, always run per request.

To cache the data behind a handler that runs per request, call a `"use cache"` function from it, like `getProduct` from the caching lesson. The directive can't go in the handler's own body. `getProduct` returns `null` for a product the API doesn't know, rather than throwing: an error thrown inside cached code loses its details in a production build, so the handler couldn't tell a missing product from a crash.

examples.title: A product endpoint
examples.prompt: `app/api/products/[slug]/route.ts`: one product as JSON, for any app that asks.
examples.explanation: The file exports one function, `GET`, so this URL answers GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS. The request itself isn't needed, so its name starts with an underscore, a common way to say unused. `ctx.params` resolves to `{ slug: "trail-pack-45" }` for `/api/products/trail-pack-45`. `getProduct` is the cached reader from the caching lesson, so most calls never reach the Trailhead API. The handler sends back four fields, not the whole product: like an action's return value, a handler's response is public, and a smaller answer is one you can change later without breaking the apps that read it. A missing product gets a 404 with a short JSON body, so a caller can tell missing apart from broken.

examples.title: Asking for a product that doesn't exist
examples.prompt: With the app running (`npm run build`, then `npm run start`), ask the endpoint for a slug the shop doesn't have.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Vary: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch, Accept-Encoding
content-type: application/json
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 03:07:31 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

{"error":"No such product"}
examples.explanation: The status line says 404, and `content-type: application/json` came from `Response.json`. The `Vary` header is Next.js's own, on every response: it tells caches that the answer depends on those request headers, which the router sends when it asks for RSC payloads. `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` means the body was sent in pieces with no length given up front, the usual way for a server that streams. Ask for `/api/products/trail-pack-45` instead, and you get `200 OK` with `{"slug":"trail-pack-45","name":"Trail Pack 45L","priceCents":18900,"inStock":true}`.

examples.title: Methods the file doesn't export
examples.prompt: Send a POST, which the file doesn't handle, then an OPTIONS, which Next.js answers for you.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
vary: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:08:10 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
vary: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch
allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:08:10 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: `-X` sets the method. The file has no `POST` export, so Next.js answers `405 Method Not Allowed` without running any of your code. For `OPTIONS`, which the file doesn't export either, Next.js answers by itself with `204 No Content` and an `allow` header listing what this URL accepts: `GET`, and the `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` that come with it. Browsers send `OPTIONS` before some cross-origin requests, which part 4 covers. When you need to control that answer, export your own `OPTIONS`.

steps.title: When a Route Handler is the right tool

examples.title: A signed webhook
examples.prompt: `app/api/webhooks/stock/route.ts`: a stock system would call it when stock changes. It checks the signature, then marks the product's cache stale.
examples.explanation: `createHmac("sha256", secret)` makes the code from the body with SHA-256, a standard recipe for such codes, and `digest("hex")` writes it as 64 hexadecimal characters, the digits 0 to 9 and the letters a to f. `timingSafeEqual` needs two byte buffers of the same length, so the lengths are compared first. A bad or missing signature gets a 401 and nothing else happens. Only after the check is the body parsed. A `stock.changed` event marks that product's cache tag stale, so the next visitor to its page triggers a fresh fetch in the background. `after` schedules the log line for after the response, which part 5 explains, and `204 No Content` tells the service the event arrived. In a real handler, also check `event` with zod, since a signed body can still be shaped wrong.

examples.title: Sending a signed event
examples.prompt: On a Mac or Linux, sign an event with the webhook secret and send it, the way a stock system would.
examples.code:
body='{"type":"stock.changed","slug":"trail-pack-45"}'
sig=$(printf '%s' "$body" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "whsec_local_only_7b1f" | awk '{print $NF}')
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3005/api/webhooks/stock -H "x-trailhead-signature: $sig" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "$body"
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
vary: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 03:07:34 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: The first line keeps the event in a shell variable. The second signs it the way a stock system would: `openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac` computes the HMAC with the same secret as `STOCK_WEBHOOK_SECRET` in `.env.local`, and `awk` keeps only the code from the end of its line. The third sends the event with the code in the `x-trailhead-signature` header. The handler answered 204, and the terminal running the app then printed webhook stock.changed for trail-pack-45 handled, from the `after` callback. Send the same request with `x-trailhead-signature: 0000` and you get `401 Unauthorized` with `{"error":"Bad signature"}`.

examples.title: Reading a stream of events
examples.prompt: Ask the events endpoint for the Trail Pack's stock and watch the events arrive.
examples.explanation: `-N` tells curl not to wait and collect the response before printing it, so each event shows up the moment it arrives: one, then a second's pause, then the next, then the stream closes after the third. Nobody bought a Trail Pack 45L in those three seconds, so the stock stayed at 14. In a page, `new EventSource("/api/stock/trail-pack-45/events")` receives the same events, and its `stock` listener could update a Client Component's state each time.

steps.title: Proxy runs before every route
steps.body:
Some rules apply to many pages at once, and before any of them renders: send visitors without a session cookie from `/account` to the login page, give every request an ID for the logs, move an old URL to its new home, or show half your visitors a new design. Writing that in every page repeats it, and it runs late, after the page has started. Proxy is one function that sees each request first.

## proxy.ts

In Next.js 16 this file is `proxy.ts`. Earlier versions called the same feature **middleware**, in a `middleware.ts` file, and you'll still meet that name in older code and articles. It was renamed because "middleware" made people expect a chain of handlers like in Express, a popular Node.js server library, and `npx @next/codemod@canary middleware-to-proxy .` renames an old one for you. A project has one `proxy.ts`, next to the `app` folder, exporting one function named `proxy`. In 16 it runs on Node.js, so Node's own modules work in it.

The function gets a NextRequest and decides what happens next:

- `NextResponse.next()` lets the request through to routing, with changed headers if you like.
- `NextResponse.redirect(url)` answers at once with a redirect, `307 Temporary Redirect` unless you pass another status.
- `NextResponse.rewrite(url)` serves a different path while the address bar keeps the original. That's how an A/B test shows two designs at one URL.
- A `Response` of your own, like `Response.json({ error: "Unauthorized" }, { status: 401 })`, answers without routing at all.

Returning nothing is the same as `NextResponse.next()`.

## Where it runs

```diagram route-handlers-and-proxy-pipeline
Proxy sees each request after the config's headers and redirects, and before routing.
```

In step 1, the headers and redirects from `next.config.ts` apply, which part 4 covers. Step 2 is proxy, which lets the request through or answers early. Step 3 is routing: files in `public/`, then the routes in `app/`, Route Handlers included. Step 4 is whatever matched. Server Actions aren't routes of their own: an action is a POST to its page's URL, so it passes through proxy on that page's path.

## matcher

With no `config.matcher`, proxy runs for every request, including each JavaScript file in `/_next/static`, each image, and the favicon. That's slow, and a redirect meant for pages can block a page's own scripts. `matcher` lists the paths proxy runs on, in the same pattern language `next.config.ts` uses: `/account/:path*` matches `/account` and everything under it. The example uses a **negative lookahead**, `(?!...)`, a piece of a regular expression that means "not followed by", to match every path except the listed ones. The matcher must be a constant, since Next.js reads it while building.

## Request headers and response headers

`NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } })` changes the headers your app sees. The example adds `x-request-id`, and a page reads it with `headers()` from `next/headers`. `response.headers.set(...)` changes the headers the browser sees. They're easy to confuse, and mixing them up can send a private value to the browser.

## Optimistic checks only

Proxy runs for every matched request, including the prefetches the router makes when a link scrolls into view, so it has to be fast. It shouldn't wait on the API or a database. The example only checks that a `th_session` cookie exists. That's an **optimistic check**: it turns the obvious case away early, so a logged-out visitor gets a redirect instead of a page shell. It can't tell a real session from a made-up one, since a cookie of `th_session=anything` passes. So the account page, and every action and handler behind it, still checks the session for real. The secrets and auth lesson builds that check, and shows why proxy is never the only one.

`"use cache"` and `"use server"` have no effect in proxy, and neither do `fetch`'s caching options, so anything it looks up costs a round trip on every request.

## A real 404 from the first visit

The routing lesson showed that a streamed page has already sent its `200` by the time it calls `notFound()`, so a slug nobody sells gets the not-found page with a `noindex` tag, not a `404` status. When the status itself must be `404` on the first visit, proxy can answer before any page starts. It can't ask the API, since it has to stay fast, but it can check the slug against a list the app already holds, like one written to a file during the build, and return a `Response` with status `404` for a slug that isn't on it. Most shops skip this: `noindex` already keeps the page out of search results, and the rendering lesson showed the second visit getting a real `404`.

examples.title: A proxy for the shop
examples.prompt: `proxy.ts`, next to `app/`: an optimistic login check for the account pages, and a request ID for everything else.
examples.explanation: A request for `/account` or anything under it, with no `th_session` cookie, is redirected to `/login` with a `next` parameter, so the login action can send the visitor back. `new URL("/login", request.url)` builds the full address from the incoming one. Every other request gets a fresh random ID, `crypto.randomUUID()`, added to the request headers the app sees and to the response headers the browser sees. When a visitor reports a problem, the ID in their response finds the matching lines in your logs. The matcher skips Next.js's built files, its image optimizer, the favicon, and the shop's `public/images` folder.

examples.title: The account page without a session
examples.prompt: Ask for the account page with no cookies. `-I` shows the status line and headers only.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 307 Temporary Redirect
location: /login?next=%2Faccount
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:08:34 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: curl sends no cookies unless you give it some, so proxy saw a visitor with no session. The answer came straight from proxy: `307 Temporary Redirect` with a `location` header, and none of the account page's code ran. `%2F` is the percent-encoded `/` from the web course, since a slash inside a query value is written that way. A browser follows the `location` by itself. Sent with a session cookie, the same request reaches the page, and the page's HTML holds the same `x-request-id` as the response header, since proxy gave both the one ID.

steps.title: Cookies, CORS, and caching headers

examples.title: What a built file and a public file get
examples.prompt: Ask for one of the build's JavaScript files, then a product photo from `public/images`.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
Accept-Ranges: bytes
Last-Modified: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:07:26 GMT
ETag: W/"573f-1a2005d5688"
Content-Type: application/javascript; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 22335
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:08:22 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400
Accept-Ranges: bytes
Last-Modified: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:04:49 GMT
ETag: W/"7e4-1a2005aefe4"
Content-Type: image/webp
Content-Length: 2020
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:08:22 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: The first file is one of the JavaScript chunks the build made, with a hash in its name. Take a name from your own page's HTML, since every build makes different ones. It gets a year and `immutable`, which tells the browser not to even ask again. The second is a photo from `public/images`, and its `Cache-Control` is the one from `next.config.ts`. Both have an `ETag`, a short fingerprint of the file, which lets a browser ask whether its copy is still good and get a 304, as the web course showed. Neither has an `x-request-id`, since the proxy's matcher skips both folders.

examples.title: A products endpoint a partner can call
examples.prompt: `app/api/products/route.ts`: the product list, with CORS headers for one partner's site.
examples.explanation: This is `app/api/products/route.ts`. `corsHeaders` returns the permission headers only for an origin on the list, and nothing for any other, so a page on another site can send the request but can't read the answer. `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `-Headers` answer the preflight's questions, and `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600` lets the browser remember the answer for ten minutes instead of asking before every request. Both methods send the same headers, since the browser checks the preflight and then the real response. `GET` reads `?category=` from `nextUrl` and filters the cached product list.

examples.title: A preflight from the partner's site
examples.prompt: Send the OPTIONS request a browser would send first, from a page on the partner's origin.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
vary: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch
vary: Origin
access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type
access-control-allow-methods: GET, OPTIONS
access-control-allow-origin: https://partner.example
access-control-max-age: 600
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:08:22 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: This is the preflight a browser on `https://partner.example` would send: an `OPTIONS` request with its `Origin` and the method it wants to use, in `Access-Control-Request-Method`. The handler named the partner's origin back, so the browser goes ahead with the real request. Header names print in lowercase because the `Headers` object that `Response` uses stores them that way, and the two `vary` lines count as one list. Send the same preflight with `Origin: https://evil.example`, and the answer is a bare `204 No Content` with no `access-control` headers, so that browser refuses to let its page read the response.

steps.title: After the response, and every server error
steps.body:
Two jobs happen around the response rather than in it. Some work shouldn't make the visitor wait: a log line, an analytics event, a message to another service. And when something breaks in production, you need to hear about it, with enough detail to fix it, while the visitor sees only an error page. `after()` handles the first, and `instrumentation.ts` the second.

## after()

`after(callback)` from `next/server` runs the callback once the response has been sent. The visitor gets their answer, and your code keeps going. The webhook in part 2 used it to log each event after its 204 went out.

It works in Server Components, Server Actions, Route Handlers, and proxy, with a few rules:

- It runs even when the response failed, after an error, a `notFound()`, or a `redirect()`, so it's a good place for a log line that must always happen.
- It doesn't make a route dynamic. In a page prerendered at build time, the callback runs at build time, or whenever the page is rendered again.
- In actions and Route Handlers, the callback can call `cookies()` and `headers()`. In a Server Component it can't, since by then rendering is over: read them while rendering, and use the values inside the callback.

On your own Node.js server, the process simply keeps running until the callback finishes. On a platform that freezes a function once its response is sent, the platform has to keep it alive, which hosts that support Next.js do. Either way, the callback gets the route's time limit, not forever.

## instrumentation.ts

`instrumentation.ts` sits next to the `app` folder, like `proxy.ts`, and connects your app to monitoring tools. It can export two functions:

- `register()` runs once when a server starts, before it answers its first request. That's where a monitoring tool's setup code goes.
- `onRequestError(error, request, context)` runs for every error the server catches while handling a request: in rendering, in a Route Handler, in an action, or in proxy. It gets the error, the request's method, path, and headers, and a context saying where it happened.

The example logs each error as one line of JSON. A real app sends it to an error tracker such as Sentry instead, a service that collects errors from every server, groups the repeats, and tells you about new ones. If `onRequestError` does anything async, await it.

When an error happens while rendering a page, a production build hides its message from the browser, since a message can hold private details. The visitor's error page gets only a digest, the short code you met in the routing lesson, and the server's log has the same digest next to the full error. When someone sends you a screenshot of an error page, the digest finds the matching line.

The terminal running the app printed these lines, the first at startup and the rest after one request to `/api/boom`, a handler that throws:

```text
instrumentation: server starting (nodejs)
⨯ Error: The stock service timed out
    at r (.next/server/chunks/_0_8qb768eg4op._.js:1:107)
{"level":"error","message":"The stock service timed out","method":"GET","path":"/api/boom","routePath":"/api/boom","routeType":"route"}
```

The first line is `register()`. Next.js printed the error and where it was thrown, a file in the build, and then `onRequestError` printed its JSON: `routePath` is the file's route and `routeType` is `route`, for a Route Handler. The caller only got a `500 Internal Server Error`, with no body.

## Tracing with OpenTelemetry

Logs say what went wrong. A **trace** says where the time went: one request, broken into timed steps like rendering, each `fetch`, and each database query. **OpenTelemetry** is the open standard for collecting traces, and Next.js already records its own steps in that format. Turning it on is a few lines in `register()`: install `@vercel/otel` and call `registerOTel("trailhead-shop")`, then point it at a tool that stores and draws traces. The deployment lesson comes back to watching an app in production.

examples.title: Logging every server error
examples.prompt: `instrumentation.ts`, next to `app/`: a line at startup, and one JSON line for each error the server catches.
examples.explanation: `register` prints one line when the server starts. `NEXT_RUNTIME` says which runtime is loading the file, `nodejs` on a Node.js server. `onRequestError` takes its type from `Instrumentation`, imported from `next`. The error arrives typed `unknown`, since JavaScript can throw anything, so the code checks that it's an `Error` before reading its message. `request.path` includes the query string, and `context.routeType` is `render` for a page, `route` for a Route Handler, `action` for a Server Action, or `proxy`. One JSON object per line is a common log format, because log tools can search and count it by field. Proxy's login check in this lesson was only optimistic. The next lesson builds the real one, along with the secrets and security headers that keep the shop safe.

recap:
- A route.ts file answers HTTP requests with Request and Response, one exported function per method, and Next.js answers OPTIONS and HEAD for you.
- A GET handler that reads nothing from its request is prerendered at build time, and one that reads the request runs every time.
- Use Route Handlers for webhooks, other apps, and files or streams, never for your own pages' data or forms.
- Verify a webhook's signature over the raw body, then revalidate with revalidateTag.
- proxy.ts runs before routing on the paths its matcher lists, for redirects, rewrites, and headers, and its auth checks are only optimistic.
- Set cookies in actions, Route Handlers, or proxy, CORS headers in the handlers other origins call, and fixed headers in next.config.ts.
- after() runs work once the response is sent, and onRequestError in instrumentation.ts sees every server error.
